newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S DE KLERK SAYS TRUTH BODY NEEDS SURGERY.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S DE KLERK SAYS TRUTH BODY NEEDS SURGERY.

text.p: Opposition leader F.W. de Klerk said on Monday radical changes were needed in South Africa's Truth Commission if it were to draft a credible version of apartheid-era abuses.

"A very serious deviation from an even-handed approach and objectivity in contravention of the law cannot be rectified by applying a few band-aids," de Klerk, leader of the National Party, told a meeting of the Cape Town Press Club.

"A serious situation exists that...can only be rectified by cutting to the bone and by a totally new situation being created where trust can be restored in the process and activities of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission."

De Klerk, whose party introduced apartheid in 1948 and dismantled it four decades later, clashed last month with Truth Commission chairman Archbishop Desmond Tutu over what the National Party called Tutu's pro-African National Congress bias.
The National Party said Tutu, who publicly complained that de Klerk had failed adequately to accept blame for apartheid abuses, had effectively already found the party guilty of atrocities.
Tutu, who was patron of an ANC-aligned group during the 1980s, denied that he or his commission was anything but even-handed. It is also mandated with investigating ANC war crimes.

But the National Party said the commission's bias had become so obvious that it was temporarily boycotting Tutu's activities. De Klerk said the party would deliver a formal letter on the issue to the commission later on Monday.

Independent political analysts have described various statements by Tutu and his commissioners as making plain they believe the ANC of President Nelson Mandela holds the moral high ground in the apartheid race war.
They said the National Party, trying to shed its image as the party of apartheid, was concerned at the capital which would be made out of the work of the commission ahead of elections in 1999.
De Klerk told the Press Club on Monday most parties were already campaigning for the election, which will mark Mandela's formal retirement from politics.
"We are focusing on our election strategy," he said. "The '99 election is less than two years away. The election campaigns from all sides have for all practical purposes already begun."
De Klerk said his party, which won about 20 percent of the vote in South Africa's first democratic election in 1994, had the support of at least 500,000 blacks.
He acknowledged some confusion had been created by recent infighting within the party which resulted in Roelf Meyer, regarded as the most liberal of the party's leaders, quitting last month.
Meyer had been heading an effort sanctioned by de Klerk to form a new broad-based political movement which would stand a credible chance of ousting the ANC in 1999.

But Meyer championed the view, unpopular with de Klerk, that the National Party had no future in its current guise and should disband as quickly as possible in order to form a new, broadly- based opposition movement.
